stories.body: Governments and website operators worldwide are rushing to patch critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used by a vast share of the web, including platforms such as WordPress and Wikipedia. Researchers using OpenAI technology uncovered flaws that could allow unauthenticated attackers to take control of web servers and steal sensitive data; security firm Wiz called them among the most severe vulnerabilities identified with AI assistance. Some governments, public bodies and major web services took systems offline as a precaution, while PHP developers urged all users to update immediately. Experts warn that poorly maintained sites may be especially exposed as technical details become public.
stories.headline: Critical PHP vulnerabilities trigger worldwide patching scramble

stories.body: Russia launched a new missile attack on Kyiv hours after the Kremlin said it was ready in principle to resume three-way talks with the United States and Ukraine. The strikes hit homes, energy infrastructure and other sites in Kyiv and elsewhere, causing deaths and injuries, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said they showed Moscow was not serious about peace. US envoy Steve Witkoff had met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg after talks with Zelenskyy, and Russian officials suggested a new round could take place in Abu Dhabi after 10 November. Zelenskyy said Ukraine could accept a ceasefire freezing the front line, with security guarantees to be negotiated afterward.
stories.headline: Russia strikes Kyiv as Moscow signals readiness to resume US-mediated peace talks

stories.body: An attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, killed a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident and injured eight people, Saudi civil aviation authorities said. Earlier, falling debris after the interception of a drone targeting an Aramco facility at the Shaybah oil field killed two more people. The attacks came amid an escalating conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, with Saudi airports and energy facilities repeatedly targeted in recent weeks. The United States ordered some diplomats and family members to leave Saudi Arabia, citing threats to civilian airports and critical infrastructure.
stories.headline: Attack on Saudi Arabia's King Fahd Airport kills two amid Houthi escalation

stories.body: French authorities have banned planned demonstrations in several cities and imposed restrictions on public gatherings in sensitive parts of Paris after student protests over school conditions broadened into violent unrest, looting and attacks on public buildings. More than 2,000 people, mostly minors, were taken into custody during the disorder. President Emmanuel Macron said legitimate grievances would be addressed but rejected claims by US President Donald Trump that migration or foreign interference was behind the unrest, calling such commentary unacceptable and foolish. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a temporary suspension of social-media platforms could be considered only under very strict conditions.
stories.headline: French cities ban protests after violent unrest

stories.body: Ireland's parliament voted 79 to 71 to remove a requirement for United Nations approval before the country can deploy military peacekeepers overseas. Opponents said the change threatens Ireland's longstanding military neutrality, though Ireland is not a NATO member and has traditionally participated in international peacekeeping missions. Supporters backed the measure despite the closely divided vote.
stories.headline: Ireland votes to end UN-approval requirement for overseas peacekeeping deployments

stories.body: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found that Facebook intentionally deceived users about the privacy and handling of their personal data. The case stemmed from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which data from Facebook users was harvested for targeted political advertising during the 2016 election. Judge Francis Mathew said a larger penalty could have been justified under state law but reduced the award to $25 billion. Meta said the ruling would make it nearly impossible to do business in New Mexico and said it expected to prevail on appeal.
stories.headline: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $25 billion over Facebook privacy deception

stories.body: Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana asked the US Supreme Court to invalidate abortion shield laws in California, Massachusetts and New York, escalating the interstate legal fight over medication abortion. The Republican-led states argue that the laws obstruct their abortion bans by protecting out-of-state providers who prescribe abortion pills through telehealth and mail them to patients in states with restrictions. It is the first direct challenge by states to the validity of such shield laws, according to a legal scholar. The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction over disputes between states but rarely takes them up.
stories.headline: Three Republican-led states ask Supreme Court to overturn Democratic abortion shield laws

stories.body: A federal judge ruled that Idaho cannot prosecute doctors who perform abortions to protect a pregnant patient's health or prevent self-harm. US District Judge B. Lynn Winmill found that Idaho's near-total abortion ban violates the Fourteenth Amendment when it bars abortions needed to prevent serious but nonfatal harm, including harm related to mental illness. The ruling does not rest on a general right to abortion, but on limits to the state's power to compel a person to suffer serious medical harm for a pregnancy. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said the state would appeal.
stories.headline: Federal judge blocks Idaho prosecutions of doctors providing health-protecting abortions

stories.body: Workers with employer-sponsored health insurance are paying hundreds of dollars more toward their premiums this year, according to KFF's 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey. Employees paid an average of $7,471 annually for family coverage, an increase of about 9%, or $621, from the previous year; workers at smaller companies were especially affected because they typically bear a larger share of costs. About 157 million Americans below retirement age rely on employer-sponsored coverage, making rising health costs a major election-year affordability issue.
stories.headline: Survey finds employer health-insurance costs continuing to climb for US workers

stories.body: Spain's Constitutional Court rejected an appeal seeking to restore voting rights to more than 160,000 people who acquired Spanish nationality under the Democratic Memory Law, often called the descendants or grandchildren law. The Supreme Court had temporarily suspended their enrollment in the overseas electoral register unless consulates establish that they are descendants of Civil War or early Franco-era exiles. The Constitutional Court said the appeal was premature because legal remedies remain before the Supreme Court, leaving the suspension in place ahead of the 29 November general election. Lawyers for affected citizens say their prospects of voting are now minimal and have challenged the measure as disproportionate.
stories.headline: Spain's Constitutional Court rejects appeal over descendants-law voters barred from elections

stories.body: Spain's conservative Popular Party released an AI-generated campaign video that imitates the images and voices of Socialist figures and people associated with the government, making them appear to admit wrongdoing. The video was framed as a response to a campaign clip by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez embracing the label of being left-wing after insults from Argentine President Javier Milei. The PP's video includes simulated versions of Begoña Gómez, former minister José Luis Ábalos, former prime minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero and others. Socialist spokesperson Rebeca Torró condemned it as a continuation of an insult-based campaign, while reports said the tactic raised questions about its legitimacy and legality.
stories.headline: Spain's PP uses AI-generated videos impersonating Socialist figures in election campaign

stories.body: The Popular Party selected Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo as number two and spokesperson Borja Sémper as number three on Alberto Núñez Feijóo's Madrid list for the 29 November general election. The party said the two represent different perspectives within a broad political project, pairing Álvarez de Toledo's harder-edged profile with Sémper's more centrist appeal. Álvarez de Toledo, formerly sixth on the Madrid list, has been elevated as the party seeks to compete for voters between the PP and Vox, while Sémper remains in the position he held in the 2023 election.
stories.headline: PP puts Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo and Borja Sémper second and third on Feijóo's Madrid ticket

stories.body: Spain and Italy agreed not to extend reciprocal border checks on flights and passenger sea links that had been in place since August, when Italy imposed controls after the arrival of thousands of migrants in Ceuta from Morocco. Spain responded with similar measures for travelers from Italy, partially suspending free movement within the Schengen area for nearly three months. The agreement followed talks between the countries' interior ministers and a meeting between Prime Ministers Pedro Sánchez and Giorgia Meloni. Both governments said they would strengthen information-sharing and other security cooperation instead of prolonging the controls.
stories.headline: Spain and Italy agree to lift border controls imposed during the Ceuta migration crisis

stories.body: Catalan President Salvador Illa and Transport Minister Óscar Puente reaffirmed that the transfer of the Rodalies commuter rail system to Catalan management will continue despite Spain's early election. The government and Renfe's board are expected to approve a program contract allowing the Generalitat to manage the service through 2028 while a new joint company is prepared. Both leaders said the transfer of the R1 line remains on course, though Puente acknowledged the election could affect its timetable. They also said new trains are expected in the first quarter of next year, while work on the network has reduced weather-related disruptions.
stories.headline: Catalonia and Renfe move to approve Rodalies operating agreement despite early election

stories.body: Barcelona's planned TMB bus strikes were called off after management and unions reached a preliminary four-year collective agreement. The deal provides more rest days, including 10 additional days next year with the possibility of three more under certain conditions, increased weekend rest and a gradual reduction of the working week to 35 hours. The agreement cancels the stoppages scheduled for this week and five additional October strike days. Bus workers had sought improvements to schedules, pay and legally required consecutive weekly rest days.
stories.headline: TMB bus strike called off after management and unions reach pre-agreement

stories.body: Barcelona's city government said it intends to maintain its political break with Israeli institutions and its aim of avoiding contracts with companies linked to settlements in occupied Palestinian territories, despite a Catalan High Court ruling that annulled provisions of a 2023 municipal declaration. Deputy mayor Maria Eugènia Gay said the city would appeal and would seek legally sound ways to preserve the declaration's objectives. She said the ruling did not require the city to reverse its institutional position or automatically pay compensation to companies that may have been excluded from public tenders.
stories.headline: Barcelona reaffirms break in relations with Israel after adverse Catalan High Court ruling

stories.body: Dutch diagnostics company Qiagen has opened a global infectious-disease diagnostics research center in Esplugues de Llobregat after investing €13 million over two years. The 8,000-square-meter facility, in a former Braun factory, replaces the company's site at the University of Barcelona Science Park and houses research, manufacturing, sales, quality and regulatory operations. It will expand production and development of the QIAstat-Dx molecular testing platform, which identifies pathogens and antibiotic-resistance markers. The center employs 240 people and supports a technology developed in Barcelona that is now sold in more than 120 countries.
stories.headline: Qiagen invests €13 million in Barcelona infectious-disease research center
